quote: Das Hermannsche Problem ist die Entzifferung von Melodien, Partituren, aller Instrumente, des Textes, allein aus der resultirenden phono- graphischen Curve.
english: Hermann's problem is the deciphering of melodies, scores, all instruments, and the text, solely from the resulting phonographic curve.
topic: General philosophical remarks on mathematics: how new sciences emerge, the role of mathematics in physics and the proposal to axiomatize mechanics and optics on the model of non-Euclidean geometry, 'Hermann's problem' of reconstructing music from a phonograph curve, and a 'hymn to the circle'.

triage.modern_statement: This is a signal-processing inverse problem: start from one single-channel recording of an acoustic signal, the phonograph groove or waveform, which is a superposition of all sound sources. From that one curve, recover its components: the melodies and pitches, the full score with note onsets and durations, the identity of each instrument, and the sung text. In modern terms this combines (a) single-channel (monaural) underdetermined source separation, in which there are more sources than observation channels; (b) automatic music transcription, meaning conversion of an audio signal into musical notation, including multi-pitch estimation and instrument recognition; and (c) recognition of lyrics or speech within music. Mathematically, the decomposition is ill-posed unless further priors or models of the sources are assumed. Examples are spectral, sparsity or dictionary models and learned models.
triage.answered_by: There is no single answer. The name very likely refers to the physiologist Ludimar Hermann of Königsberg, Hilbert's own university, who analysed phonograph curves of vowels from about 1890. Today the task is spread across the research fields of automatic music transcription and single-channel blind source separation. These fields have produced many partial solutions, from NMF and sparse dictionary methods to deep learning, but the full task Hilbert describes has not been fully solved. I found no source linking this specific note to a published Hilbert problem, and it is not among the 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Ludimar Hermann (1838–1914) was a German physiologist and speech scientist who used the Edison phonograph to test theories of vowel production. This makes him the likely 'Hermann' of the note.
Professor Ludimar Hermann, of Königsberg, began studying phonograph traces around 1890 using the wax-cylinder phonograph. This is the same time and the same university as Hilbert.

Automatic Music Transcription, the design of algorithms that convert acoustic music signals into music notation, is described as a challenging task. Transcribing non-Western music is still called an open problem.
A dedicated review covers the challenges and future directions of automatic music transcription, confirming it is still an unsolved research area.

Monaural (single-channel) blind separation of polyphonic music is underdetermined. With multiple channels it becomes easier and can reduce to finding an unmixing matrix. The single-curve case Hilbert describes is the hard case.
Single-channel blind source separation of underdetermined mixtures is still an active research topic in recent work, for example using multi-encoder autoencoders.

triage.why: Hilbert's phrasing amounts to recovering every source (instruments, voice and text) and a symbolic score from one mixed waveform. That is exactly single-channel source separation plus automatic music transcription. Current reviews still describe both as challenging, with some parts openly called open problems, and both have active literatures. Identifying 'Hermann' as Ludimar Hermann is an inference: the timing, the shared university with Hilbert and the phonograph-curve topic all match, but I found no source that explicitly links him to Hilbert's note. Confidence is medium because I could not find any historical source discussing this diary entry itself, and because the problem is an engineering and inverse-problem programme rather than a single crisp theorem.
